text: Title: snpR: user friendly population genomics for SNP datasets with categorical metadata 1 Running Title: snpR: user friendly population genomics 2 1. Department of Animal Science, University of California, Davis, USA, 95616 5 The analysis of genomic data can be an intimidating process, particularly for researchers 9 who are not experienced programmers. Commonly used analyses are spread across many 10 programs, each requiring their own specific input formats, and so data must often be repeatedly 11 reorganized and transformed into new formats. Analyses often require splitting data according to 12 metadata variables such as population or family, which can be challenging to manage in large 13 datasets. Here, we introduce snpR, a user-friendly data analysis package in R for processing SNP 14 genomic data. snpR is designed to automate data sub-setting and analyses across categorical 15 metadata while also streamlining repeated analyses by integrating approaches contained in many 16 different packages in a single ecosystem. snpR facilitates iterative and efficient analyses centered 17 on a single R object for an entire analysis pipeline. 18 R packages, population genomics, population genetics, bioinformatics 20 The volume of Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) data being generated by 22 population and quantitative geneticists has exponentially grown over the last several decades. This has necessitated the development of new analytical tools, as data analysis pipelines 24 previously used for small numbers of genetic markers are not well suited for usage with many 25 thousands of SNPs. Since data sets require correspondingly large computation power, the 26 analysis of genetic and genomic data has drifted towards more efficient command line tools and 27 away from more user-friendly tools. The resulting analytical landscape, however, can be 28 daunting for researchers not well versed in bioinformatics. For example, while toolkits like 29 Stacks (Catchen, Hohenlohe, Bassham, Amores, & Cresko, 2013), SAMtools (Li et al., 2009), 30 and ANGSD (Korneliussen, Albrechtsen, & Nielsen, 2014) provide relatively user-friendly ways 31 to analyze enormous amounts of sequence data, they require users to have expertise with UNIX 32 For many researchers, the R programming language (Team, 2013) is a more welcoming 34 environment. In ecology, for example, R use has risen linearly over the last decade: more than 35 55% of papers published in the field cited R as their primary analysis tool in 2017 (Lai, Lortie, 36 Muenchen, Yang, & Ma, 2019). Thankfully, an array of R packages for the analysis of genetic 37 data exist, including general packages that cover a broad range of analysis methods (Archer, 38 Adams, & Schneiders, 2017; Gruber, Unmack, Berry, & Georges, 2018; Jombart, 2008; Paradis, 39 2010; Paradis, Claude, & Strimmer, 2004) and packages dedicated to single analyses such as 40 Random Forest regressions (Wright & Ziegler, 2017), genomic prediction (Pérez & Campos, 41 2014), relatedness matrix construction (Amadeu et al., 2016), Genome Wide Association Studies 42 (GWAS) (Chen, 2020), spatial ecological genetics (Frichot & François, 2015), hierarchical Fௌ் 43 calculation (Jérôme Goudet, 2005), among others. However, these packages generally require a 44 relatively high level of fluency in R, as data needs to be wrangled into multiple specific data 45 formats or repeatedly split based on sample or loci classification, such as population or 46 chromosome. This problem is compounded by the disparate nature of these analytical tools, as a 47 basic population genetic analysis will likely require the use of several tools, each with their own 48 data format requirements and syntactical quirks. Here we present snpR, a new R package for the analysis of SNP population genomic 50 data, aims to simplify and centralize genomic analysis to maximize ease-of-use. snpR is designed 51 to meet three analytical goals: 1) automate the separation of samples and loci around facets of the 52 data without the need to manually split datasets; 2) be non-destructive, such that subsequent 53 analyses, broken up by whatever facets a particular analysis requires, are all applied and saved in 54 a single object, reducing the organizational burden of version management and improving the 55 readability and reproducibility of scripts while providing a convenient means of appropriate 56 tracking attribution for methods citations; and 3) condense statistical methods and data 57 visualization from a large range of genetic toolkits into a single package. 58 snpR is built to accept both raw tab-delimited genotypic data (in, for example, NN, 0/1/2, 61 or 0000 formats like those used by the ANGSD software package (Korneliussen et al., 2014), 62 BGLR (Pérez & Campos, 2014), or genepop (Rousset, 2008)), and can convert from adegenet 63 genind objects (Jombart, 2008), and read plink (Purcell et al., 2007), genepop (Rousset, 2008), 64 ms (Hudson, 2002), STRUCTURE (Pritchard, Stephens, & Donnelly, 2000), or FSTAT (J. 65 Goudet, 1995) input files (see Table 1). snpR offers a range of helper import and conversion 66 functions (such as read_vcf and convert_genind) to make the import process as painless as 67 Unlike other population genomics toolkits, snpR simultaneously stores unlimited 69 columns of both SNP and sample metadata for easy access, filtering, and analysis. Each import 70 function therefore takes an optional data.frame or file paths that either contain or point to tab71 delimited SNP and sample metadata sets. This allows users to more dynamically filter, access, 72 and analyze complex multi-faceted data. For example, users can filter and run analyses by 73 combining sample population, family group, phenotype, or any number of other metadata 74 variables simultaneously (see Figure 1 and Figure 2). snpR can export data into a range of 75 possible formats including but not limited to each of those discussed above (see Table 2). 76 snpR is built from the ground up to prioritize ease of use and avoid computational 78 redundancy. It principally achieves this goal by storing collected genotypic data, metadata, and 79 computed statistics and summaries in a single modifiable snpRdata object to which additional 80 analyses can be iteratively added (see Figure 2). Internally, snpR automatically calculates a range 81 of basic summary information when initializing a snpRdata object, such as allele/genotype 82 frequency tables. During analysis, statistical functions add to and return snpRdata objects rather 83 than returning raw statistical results directly. Additional statistics, such as observed 84 heterozygosity (Hை), expected heterozygosity (Hா), nucleotide diversity (π), or Fௌ், are 85 calculated and stored internally for both dynamic user access and later re-use. As such, snpR 86 calculations are almost never redundant: for example, if a user first calculates Hை for each SNP, 87 those numbers can then be directly (and automatically) re-used if the user later calculates Weir 88 and Cockerham’s (1984) Fௌ். Functions will automatically generate both per-SNP values and 89 The iterative nature of snpR also has a convenient side-benefit of allowing for the 91 automatic tracking and reporting of citations for methods used during analyses. Each snpR 92 function is built to update an internal tracker of utilized methods, which can be used to produce a 93 report detailing the sources for each method used during analysis or it can export a bibtex (.bib) 94 file which can then be imported to a citation manager. This should streamline searching citations 95 for the methods they use and aids proper attribution–instead of citing just snpR alone, snpR 96 encourages users to cite the actual developers of the methods that snpR implements. This iterative approach, alongside the snpR’s sizable methodological suite, also supports 98 reproducible research. As sequential statistical methods are all run on a single object, analyses 99 using snpR can avoid the need to track, update, and organize multiple input files for multiple 100 programs or objects for different packages. This should make analyses generally easy to interpret 101 for interested researchers, readers, and reviewers. 102 snpR is designed from the ground up to facilitate the easy analysis of data separated by 104 one or more categorical variables in both SNP and sample metadata simultaneously without 105 manual data separation by use of the facets argument provided to any snpR function. For 106 example, there is no need to create different sets of objects or inputs if the user wishes to try 107 calculating diversity statistics by population, family, or sample year. Instead, the user can simply 108 refer to different columns in the sample metadata by name using a straightforward syntax (see 109 the “Use Example” section below and Figure 1). No manual separation of data is ever required, 110 and snpR functions are built to automatically handle the facets argument in an identical way 111 unless the specific method prohibits it (such as some plotting tools). Facets can refer to single or 112 any combination of metadata columns in either the SNP or sample metadata (see Figure 1). As 113 before, statistics calculated by facet are stored in the same iterative snpRdata object, which 114 allows for straightforward, easy-to-read, easy-to-write, and easy-to-replicate analyses. 115 snpR implements a large range of genetic methods both natively and via interface with 118 external packages and programs. This includes basic SNP filtering, genetic diversity calculation 119 (π /expected heterozygosity, observed heterozygosity, Tajima’s D (Tajima, 1989), site frequency 120 spectra (SFS), bootstrapping, pairwise Linkage Disequilibrium, etc.), population divergence and 121 structuring (pairwise Fௌ், two-dimensional SFS, directionality index (Peter & Slatkin, 2013), and 122 R interfaces for STRUCTURE or ADMIXTURE (Alexander & Lange, 2011; Pritchard et al., 123 2000) clustering analysis), association testing, genomic prediction and heritability estimation, 124 parentage/pedigree construction, and many others (see Table 3 for all available methods). While this set of analysis tools is not comprehensive, it is more complete than other 126 currently available R packages, and will continue to grow as users request additional methods 127 implementations. As it stands currently, this package provides access to analytical tools covering 128 the basic needs of most population genomics projects. All functions are written to take similar 129 input arguments and, when possible, integrate results into the input snpRdata object for ease of 130 use. For analyses not available in snpR, a range of data conversion options are available, making 131 for a quick and easy transition into analyses in other commonly used programs (see Table 2). 132 snpR comes with built in functions to generate ggplot2-compatible visualizations 134 (Wilkinson, 2011). For example, snpR can generate STRUCTURE style plots from 135 STRUCTURE output-like files (via interface with the pophelper package Francis, 2017) or by 136 running STRUCTURE (Pritchard et al., 2000), ADMIXTURE (Alexander & Lange, 2011), or 137 sNMF directly (Frichot, Mathieu, Trouillon, Bouchard, & François, 2014)), plot pairwise linkage 138 disequilibrium, run and plot Principal Component Analyses (PCA), phylogenetic trees via 139 interface with the ape (Paradis & Schliep, 2018) and ggtree (Yu, Smith, Zhu, Guan, & Lam, 140 2017) packages, manhattan association plots, and others. 141 Statistical outputs can be generated via the get.snpR.stats function for any facets of 142 interest. Both per-snp values and population means are automatically returned when applicable 143 snpR is written almost entirely in optimized R code. All functions are vectorized where 146 possible and allow for parallel processing via the foreach (Wallig, Corporation, & Weston, 2020) 147 and doParallel (Wallig, Corporation, Weston, & Tenenbaum, 2020) packages wherever doing so 148 can speed up processes. Data management uses the data.table package (Dowle, Srinivasan, Short, 149 & Lianoglou, 2017) to reduce storage size, processing times, and read/write times. As such, it 150 can run complex native operations quickly, and competes favorably with many other commonly 151 used R packages (for comparison, snpR was faster than the “pegas”, “strataG”, and “dartR” 152 packages for Hா, Hardy-Weinburg Equilibrium, and Fௌ் calculation, and snpR was faster than 153 everything except dartR for Hை calculation with 10,000 loci across 204 samples from 12 154 populations on an Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-10750H 2.60GHz CPU with 16 GB of available RAM; 155 see Table 4; Paradis (2010); Gruber et al. 156 snpR includes example datasets for Three-spined Stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) 159 from the Deschutes River, Oregon, USA (Hemstrom, 2016). The objects stickSNPs and 160 stickRAW contain data stored in the “NN” format, where each SNP is a row and each individual 161 a column. Each also have three header columns of SNP metadata. In the following example, the sample metadata is stored in another tab-delimited file 163 named “sample_metadata.txt”, which can be read in alongside genotypes directly with the 164 read_delimited_snps helper function. There are no required columns in either metadata file, and 165 these arguments can also be left blank if no metadata is available. If the SNP metadata was in a different file instead, we could provide a path to that using 167 the snp.meta argument instead of the header_cols argument. Note that data can also be read from 168 a range of other formats with different helper functions. If sample or snp metadata are not 169 directly provided, snpR will try to locate them in the file or object (see Table 1 for a full list of 170 dat <- read_vcf("exdat.vcf", sample.meta = "sample_metadata.txt") # VCF 172 dat <- read_genepop("exdat.pop", snp.meta = "snp_metadata.txt") # genepop 173 dat <- read_plink("exdat") # plink, no extension 174 dat <- convert_genind(genind = genind_obj) # adegenet genind object 175 All of these methods are implemented in the function import.snpR.data, which will 176 automatically guess the appropriate input format and can also work with pre-existing 177 snpR also offers a inbuilt filtering function (filter_snps) with a range of options, such as 182 removing poorly sequenced individuals or loci or removing loci with a low minor allele 183 frequency or that are not in Hardy Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) either across the entire dataset 184 hwe = 0.0001, # remove snps with HWE p-val < 0.0001 189 min_ind = .5, # remove samples missing > 50% of genotypes 191 min_loci = .5) # remove loci missing > 50% of genotypes 192 While snpR is set up to minimize the need for subsetting or re-arrangement of data, 194 manually removing or subsetting samples or SNPs is nonetheless straightforward. Data can be 195 subset using the usual “[“ operators by numeric index (as with most R objects) or via reference to 196 metadata columns. Negative subsetting is also supported, and the data can be subset by multiple 197 # keep samples in the ASP population and the A family 206 Statistics in snpR are calculated iteratively by updating the original snpR object as more 209 statistic are calculated, rather than sending the results of each calculation to separate outputs (See 210 Figure 2). This is done to reduce computational redundancy, increase ease-of-use, and improve 211 reproducibility. For example, to calculate π (nucleotide diversity), Hை, and overall Fூௌ, the 212 calc_pi, calc_ho, and calc_fis functions can be called successively on the same object. 213 The results can then be fetched in a human readable form using the get.snpR.stats helper 217 res <- get.snpR.stats(dat, stats = c("pi", "ho", "fis")) 219 snpR is built to support the easy calculation of statistics split by metadata categories or 220 combinations of metadata categories via the facets argument by referring to the columns of 221 Note that since any previously calculated statistics needed by subsequent functions are 227 saved in the same object, they do not need to be recalculated. For example, Wier and 228 Cockerham’s (1984) Fௌ் requires Hை. If Hை has been previously calculated for the same facet, as 229 in the above example, snpR can compute Fௌ் more quickly by simply fetching the statistics the 230 Multiple columns of interest can be used at once. For example, to calculate statistics for 232 each unique combination of population (pop) and family (fam) simultaneously. Alternatively, we can run each facet separately using c() to split independently once by 237 Statistics can also be computed with reference to SNP metadata. For example, calc_pi 242 can be used to calculate the average π for each chromosome in each population. Note that there 243 is no need to tell snpR where to look for metadata (SNP or sample). Note that throughout this example, the same object, dat, was repeatedly overwritten. At 246 this point, dat contains information on all of the statistics and facets we ran, since snpR functions 247 return snpRdata objects with additional results merged in. Since it is not significantly more computationally expensive to 256 calculate averages for multiple statistics, windowed averages will be automatically calculated for 257 any previously run statistics. Bootstrapped p-values for each window can later be calculated 258 using do_bootstraps. Note that many of these analyses can also be run in parallel using the par = 259 snpR also interfaces with several commonly used external (non-R) tools using identical 265 syntax to other snpR functions whenever possible. Any parameter tweaks the user may wish to use are passed 267 as arguments to calc_ne. 268 dat <- calc_ne(dat, facets = "pop", 269 chr = "chr", # don't use LD between SNPs on the same chr! 270 snpR offers a range of plotting tools to visualize population structuring and diversity. For 273 example, snpR contains tools to interpolate missing genotypes and run a PCA, coloring 274 individuals by facet (see Figure 3). The resulting object is a ggplot2 plot, and so is modifiable 275 STRUCTURE-like plots can also be created (see Figure 4), either directly or by 279 importing “.qopt” files from other programs, and the results can be easily plotted on maps. snpR 280 supports several methods directly internally or via interface (see Table 3): 281 • Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (sNMF) (Frichot et al., 2014) 282 • snapclust (Beugin, Gayet, Pontier, Devillard, & Jombart, 2018) 285 snpR will automatically sort individuals by cluster membership proportions within the 287 final cluster to help make the visualization cleaner, although this behavior can be disabled using 288 either the qsort = or qsort_k Many repetitions and k values can be run 289 simultaneously and the results can be collapsed using CLUMPP. snpR uses the pophelper 290 package to help handle and read qfiles (Francis, 2017). sNMF in particular is implemented in R 291 via the LEA package (Frichot et al., 2014), and so runs without the need for any other 292 executables. Like for all of snpR’s plotting tools, sNMF parameters (such as α or the number of 293 iterations) and plotting options can be tweaked with arguments. 294 x <- plot_structure(dat, facet = "pop", k = 5, method = "snmf") 295 STRUCTURE-like results can also be easily plotted on a simple feature (sf) class map 297 Several other plotting tools are available in snpR: 299 • Basic diagnostic plots for data missingness, allele frequency spectra, and Fூௌ. 300 • Pairwise Linkage Disequilibrium via plot_pairwise_LD_heatmap. 302 snpR is built to allow for easy citation handling in order to help users properly cite the 308 methods that they used while running analyses in the snpR package. To fetch the citations used 309 on a snpRdata object, use the citations function. The outbib = argument can be used to generate a .bib (bibtex) file for import into a 316 citation manager. Plots that don’t return snpRdata objects (such as plotting tools) can instead 317 update an existing .bib file using the update_bib = argument. 318 Many R packages exist for conducting various population genomics analyses. While this 320 means that R’s genetic toolkit is expansive, it is also disparate: researchers will nearly always 321 need to install and use several packages to complete a most population genetics analyses. For 322 example, packages like pegas (Paradis, 2010), adegenet (Jombart, 2008), dartR (Gruber et al., 323 2018) and snpRelate (Zheng et al., 2012) provide many tools for conducting population 324 genomics analyses. However, each of these packages have fairly specialized target areas for 325 analyses, and users of these packages may need to find and use additional tools to complete all of 326 the analyses required for a project. Unfortunately, even determining exactly what analyses can be 327 completed with some packages can be difficult as documentation may be incomplete, and 328 statistics can have differing names or abbreviations across packages. As a result, R based population genetics has a steep learning curve, at it can be difficult to 330 manage formatting and syntax requirements for all of the packages a researcher might use for a 331 single project. snpR collects a large set of methods under a single umbrella than any other single 332 package via a mix of native implementations for many commonly used analyses and 333 syntactically consistent wrappers for other packages (See Table 1). For more niche uses, snpR 334 provides a quick and easy way to export data in various formats without even the need to use 335 other external conversion tools such as PGDspider (Lischer & Excoffier (2011); see Table 2 for 336 snpR is also built upon a foundation of reproducible research. While most population 338 genetics projects will calculate a similar suite of statistics (such as Fௌ், effective population size 339 (Nா), or Hை), there are several different methods for calculating many of these, and keeping track 340 of exactly how a particular statistic is implemented in each package can pose a challenge, 341 especially when someone may want to reproduce prior work. For example, Genome-Wide 342 Association Study (GWAS)-style association testing has four methods implemented in snpR 343 alone, with countless other alternatives available. To aid in reproducibility and clarity, snpR 344 automatically tracks and reports references for any statistics used as analyses are completed. Of course, snpR is not exhaustive and cannot include every existing method that a 346 researcher may wish to implement. As it stands, snpR implements most methods commonly used 347 for population genomics research projects and some less commonly seen but extremely useful 348 features such as random forest, genomic prediction, and sliding windows. In total, snpR contains 349 more unique methods than any of the other 20+ R-based packages we reviewed (See 350 Supplementary Table S1). Unique to snpR (to the best of our knowledge) are directionality 351 (Peter & Slatkin, 2013), citation tracking, STRUCTURE result mapping, and simultaneous 352 calculations of statistics across any number of facets. 353 snpR offers users a toolkit for the analysis of SNP data that is designed from the ground 355 up for ease of use and flexibility. By implementing or linking to a range of analysis methods and 356 allowing automatic splitting of data and citation tracking, snpR allows users to complete a 357 reproducible, basic population genomic analysis in a single platform without complicated data 358 snpR can currently be downloaded from github using the remotes package.
